## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{100}}
\end{marginfigure}

_What indelible signatures does physical hardware leave in recorded datasets, and why does treating robotic teleoperation like disembodied web scraping guarantee deployment failure?_

In traditional disembodied machine learning, datasets are treated as collections of independent and identically distributed samples mined from static web text or curated image repositories. Data pipelines focus on tokenization throughput, deduplication, and distributed sharding under the assumption that samples are passive, read-only bitstrings reproducible at zero marginal hardware cost. Scraping another billion tokens incurs server electrical utility costs, but it leaves the external world unaltered and inflicts zero mechanical damage. In Physical AI, every recorded byte of sensor observation and actuator telemetry is an active, irreversible physical intervention in the physical world. A teleoperation dataset does not capture pure, disembodied task semantics; it permanently records the motor gear lash, sensor exposure latencies, human operator reaction delays, thermal drift, and surface friction of a specific physical machine operating at a specific moment in space and time. When a neural policy trains on these trajectories, it absorbs these latent mechanical properties as causal priors. Naively aggregating multi-robot datasets without accounting for camera mount extrinsics, motor frequency response mismatches, or microsecond clock jitter causes policies to overfit to hardware quirks rather than learning generalized manipulation skills.

Furthermore, physical data pipelines face severe economic and physical bottlenecks. Unlike digital logs, physical data is scarce, hazardous to collect, consumes irreversible component fatigue life on strain-wave gears and wiring harnesses, and is throttled by human operator fatigue and mechanical scene reset delays. Under realistic facility constraints, less than one quarter of scheduled recording hours yields validated demonstration data. Every unmodeled shift in ambient illumination, floor traction, or battery charge alters the governing physical transfer function. This chapter formalizes physical data engineering as a rigorous cyber-physical systems co-design discipline. We trace how physical transduction artifacts propagate into learned representations, establish rigorous data cleaning and microsecond-level time-synchronization protocols across the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP), and demonstrate how to structure multimodal sensor logs into standardized, reproducible datasets that generalize across disparate robotic bodies.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Estimate usable demonstration yield from collection time, operator rest, and physical reset overhead, and budget the mechanical component wear a campaign consumes
- Analyze why endogenous covariate shift produces quadratic compounding error ($O(T^2\epsilon)$) and how the collecting policy limits dataset coverage
- Separate failed autonomous actions from human recovery trajectories across the divergence and takeover timestamps in intervention records
- Evaluate whether an embodiment's mechanical, sensing, and timing assumptions transfer to another machine without falling into the normalization fallacy
- Design an immutable demonstration provenance record linking each observation to its four-stream action taps ($a_{\text{req}}, a_{\text{cmd}}, a_{\text{enf}}, a_{\text{meas}}$) and to the collecting plant
- Assess whether a dataset supports a claimed operational design domain by joining its empirical state-action occupancy against a scenario ledger

:::

## Endogenous Experience {#sec-data-endogenous-experience}

Part I established the physical anatomy of the embodied machine: its causal boundary (@sec-boundary), actuator torque-thermal envelopes (@sec-body), heterogeneous compute hierarchy (@sec-brain), and real-time fieldbuses (@sec-nervous). Yet a machine with fully characterized anatomy remains inert without a behavioral policy. In Part II, we begin teaching the machine. Unlike disembodied machine learning systems that train on web-scraped text corpora or static image repositories, an embodied agent learns from physical telemetry harvested directly through its sensors and actuators. In disembodied machine learning systems, the data pipeline is strictly open-loop: scraping web text or caching static vision datasets does not alter the underlying data sources, and model predictions never mutate the training distribution retroactively. In Physical AI, data generation is fundamentally closed-loop and endogenous.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense node."}

*The Sense axis: harvesting physical experience through multimodal sensory telemetry.*
:::

A policy trained on the retained demonstrations of a door-opening campaign—clean teleoperated openings of the warehouse mobile manipulator's spring-latched cage door—can still fail at the latch on its first autonomous attempt. One fundamental cause is the shift the machine's own actions create.[^fn-data-causal-loop] In a fixed offline vision dataset, the model's prediction does not change the next stored example. In an embodied Markov Decision Process (MDP), an executed action changes the body's physical trajectory, camera pose, and contact states, thereby altering the distribution of all subsequent observations ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$).

[^fn-data-causal-loop]: **Causal Boundary**\index{Causal boundary!thermodynamic constraint}: The causal boundary between computation and physics is established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary. Because state evolution depends on motor actuation, policy actions perturb the distribution of future observations, which breaks the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption of disembodied machine learning.

::: {#dfn-data-endogenous-covariate-shift .callout-definition title="Endogenous covariate shift"}

***Endogenous covariate shift***\index{Endogenous covariate shift!definition}\index{Covariate drift!physical AI} is the closed-loop distribution discrepancy wherein an embodied agent's executed actions alter its subsequent physical states and sensory observations ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$), driving the system into state-space regimes unsupported by its training demonstrations.

1.  **Significance**: Explains how offline behavioral cloning can fail during closed-loop physical execution: a perturbation may drive the system into states where the policy lacks training support.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike exogenous dataset shift caused by changing ambient lighting or seasonal weather, endogenous shift is actively generated by the agent's own closed-loop actions altering its subsequent observation distribution.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Attempting to fix closed-loop policy failure by collecting more nominal expert demonstrations, which only increases data density along the success manifold without providing the corrective recovery data needed to escape boundary excursions.

:::

This shift is the collection-side face of principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}. It makes an archive of flawless executions without recovery trajectories an operational liability, because the policy's first mistake moves the robot outside the demonstrated states.

### Mechanics of endogenous covariate shift {#sec-data-covariate-shift}

In classical statistical learning theory, empirical risk minimization assumes that samples are drawn independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) from an exogenous, stationary distribution $\mathcal{D}$. An image classifier that misidentifies a dog as a cat does not alter the pixels of subsequent images in the test set. In passive machine learning, covariate shift typically refers to changes in the marginal input distribution $P(X)$ while the conditional label distribution $P(Y \mid X)$ remains stationary—for instance, evaluating an image classifier trained on sunny daytime driving under rainy nighttime illumination. In Physical AI, however, the shift is not merely passive or perceptual; it is an active **physical dynamics shift**. The governing physical plant is a continuous dynamical system whose differential equations $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{plant}})$ mutate as a direct consequence of operation. As actuators execute commands, Joule heating ($I^2 R$) elevates motor winding temperatures by $40\text{--}60^\circ\text{C}$, increasing copper resistance and attenuating available motor torque; cyclic friction across strain-wave gears shears lubricants and increases joint backlash; compliant silicone gripper pads wear down, altering contact friction cones and compliance; and manipulated workpieces exhibit unmodeled variations in mass, center of gravity, and surface roughness across trials.

In embodied control, the policy's actions induce an *endogenous state visitation distribution* $d^\pi(s)$. When a policy trains via offline behavioral cloning on demonstrations generated by an expert policy $\pi^*$, it minimizes imitation loss over the expert's occupancy distribution $d^{\pi^*}(s)$. During autonomous execution, however, the policy must generate actions under its own induced distribution $d^\pi(s)$. The divergence between $d^{\pi^*}$ and $d^\pi$ produces a catastrophic compounding of errors over time.

### The continuous curse of dimensionality and the recoverability problem {#sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability}

To understand why error compounds quadratically ($T^2\epsilon$), one must examine the geometry of physical state-action spaces. An embodied robot operates across continuous, high-dimensional spaces: the state $\mathbf{s} \in \mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^{d_s}$ comprises joint coordinates, angular velocities, motor drive currents, multi-axis contact wrenches, and multi-view pixel rasters, while the action $\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^{d_a}$ commands continuous joint velocities or motor torques. Unlike discrete natural language processing where vocabulary tokens form a finite set and large corpora provide dense transitions across semantic graphs, the continuous physical interaction manifold is uncountably infinite. A human teleoperator demonstrating a manipulation task traces an infinitesimally thin, one-dimensional trajectory thread through this continuous space.

Because human demonstrators are skilled, they remain centered along the optimal path on every recorded run. The resulting dataset contains thousands of frames showing the nominal trajectory, but zero frames showing what the scene looks like when the chassis or gripper drifts 15 millimeters off-track toward an obstacle or fixture. This creates the **recoverability problem**:

1. **Zero support outside the nominal tube**: The offline demonstration archive provides dense empirical support exclusively along the success manifold ($d^{\pi^*}(s) > 0$), leaving the surrounding neighborhood completely unvisited ($d^{\pi^*}(s) = 0$).
2. **Ungrounded off-manifold extrapolation**: When the learned policy takes control, an unmodeled friction variation, voltage ripple, or single-step prediction error $\epsilon$ pushes the physical plant off the demonstrated manifold. Lacking demonstrations for that state, the policy's neural network emits ungrounded, arbitrary actions.
3. **Absence of corrective vectors**: Because the policy was never shown how to steer back from off-nominal states toward the nominal tube, its arbitrary action carries the plant further away from the task manifold, converting a minor tracking error into an irreversible collision, stall, or joint limit trip.

We can derive the resulting quadratic error scaling from basic discrete summation. Suppose an agent makes an execution error at step $t \in \{1, \dots, T\}$ with probability $\epsilon$. Prior to step $t$, the agent traversed the expert trajectory with zero error. At step $t$, the single-step deviation drives the physical plant off the demonstrated manifold into an unvisited state. Because the offline dataset contains zero corrective demonstrations for off-nominal states, the agent lacks the recovery policies required to return to the nominal path, incurring a task penalty for every remaining step in the horizon ($T - t$). Under a normalized unit cost ($c_t = 1$) for unrecovered states, the expected cumulative penalty incurred across the entire trajectory sums to:
$$\sum_{t=1}^T \epsilon (T - t) = \epsilon \left( T^2 - \sum_{t=1}^T t \right) = \epsilon \left( T^2 - \frac{T(T+1)}{2} \right) = \frac{T(T-1)}{2} \epsilon \approx \frac{1}{2} T^2 \epsilon.$$
Contrast this result with open-loop supervised prediction: if errors at each step were independent and did not alter future inputs, an $\epsilon$ per-step error rate would accumulate linearly over $T$ steps as $\sum_{t=1}^T \epsilon = T\epsilon$. The extra factor of $T$ in $\mathcal{O}(T^2\epsilon)$ is the mathematical signature of closed-loop endogenous feedback.

This discrete compounding reflects a foundational physical law of motion. In Newtonian mechanics, an uncorrected actuation error (such as a torque deficit, friction mismatch, or steering bias) produces an instantaneous acceleration error $\Delta a = \Delta F / m$. Integrating acceleration once over time yields a linearly expanding velocity drift $\Delta v(t) = \int \Delta a \, dt = \Delta a \cdot t$. Integrating velocity a second time yields a spatial trajectory divergence that expands quadratically with elapsed time:
$$\Delta x(t) = \iint \Delta a \, dt^2 = \frac{1}{2} \Delta a \, t^2.$$
In physical space, an uncorrected perturbation drifts as $t^2$ even before evaluating task loss. On robots manipulating rigid objects or traversing narrow corridors, this quadratic spatial excursion rapidly drives the machine past the narrow physical basin of attraction where nominal control remains feasible.

Formally, let $\pi$ be the learned policy, $\pi^*$ the expert, $J$ expected cumulative task cost over $T$ steps, and $\epsilon$ the probability of disagreement on expert-visited states under 0–1 action loss: $\mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^{\pi^*}} [\mathbb{I}(\pi(s) \ne \pi^*(s))] \le \epsilon$. If per-step task cost lies in $[0,1]$, behavioral cloning admits the rigorous worst-case bound (@eq-data-quadratic-drift) derived by @ross2011reduction:
$$J(\pi)-J(\pi^*) \le T^2\epsilon.$$ {#eq-data-quadratic-drift}

It is essential to recognize the physical meaning and limits of this bound. If a manipulation episode runs for $T = 500$ steps with cost $c_t \in [0, 1]$, the maximum physically possible cumulative cost is $500 \times 1 = 500$. If the policy has an error rate of $\epsilon = 0.01$ (1 percent error), the quadratic formula yields $T^2\epsilon = 500^2 \times 0.01 = 2500$, which exceeds the physical maximum cost by a factor of 5! The formal bound is strictly $\min(T, T^2\epsilon)$, where the quadratic regime holds while cumulative divergence is small ($T\epsilon \ll 1$). The practical lesson for systems engineers is that without recovery demonstrations, even tiny single-step errors ($\epsilon = 0.001$) cascade so quickly that the system reaches catastrophic failure long before the planned task horizon concludes.[^fn-ai-covariate-shift]

[^fn-ai-covariate-shift]: **Behavioral Cloning Bound**\index{Covariate shift!endogenous feedback}\index{Behavioral cloning!quadratic error compounding}: The bound derived by @ross2011reduction is a worst case on expected cumulative cost, not a prediction of tracking error; actual drift depends on the plant, task, policy, and safeguards. @Sec-appendix-ml-compounding derives the bound and states its loss and bounded-cost assumptions.

Crucially, attempting to resolve endogenous covariate shift by simply recording more nominal expert demonstrations—the *nominal demonstration trap*—is fundamentally flawed. Adding another thousand hours of clean, centered demonstrations increases sample density along the nominal trajectory, but the empirical support outside the nominal tube remains strictly zero ($d^{\pi^*}(s) = 0$). Furthermore, gathering physical experience is governed by harsh physical economics. Unlike web crawlers that ingest static text asynchronously at zero marginal hardware depreciation, every recorded second of physical robotics telemetry consumes actuator fatigue life, heats motor windings ($dT/dt$), cycles gearbox teeth, and drains the battery.[^fn-data-hardware-wear] Human operator fatigue, sensor recalibrations, automated scene resets, and rejected trials leave less than one quarter of scheduled facility cell time as validated demonstration data (@sec-data-teleop-costs). Physical demonstration data is scarce and expensive; logging it without accounting for closed-loop dynamics misleads policy training.

[^fn-data-hardware-wear]: **Hardware Fatigue Life**\index{Hardware wear!actuator thermal duty cycle}: Actuator thermal limits and gearbox wear, detailed in @sec-body-actuator-limits and @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles, change joint friction over a campaign, so a pipeline that assumes stationary plant dynamics meets drift as the collection machine ages.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Actuator thermal dissipation ($dT/dt$) and winding damage limits are derived in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.
:::

A physical command also changes meaning on its way to the actuators. In a machine divided by the proposal boundary,[^fn-data-proposal-permission] the operator's or policy's request is mapped into a setpoint, admitted or modified by the permission path, and answered by the plant with a measured response. Logging only the request trains the policy on demands the plant could never execute, and logging only the response teaches it structural deflection and gear backlash as though they were deliberate human skill.

[^fn-data-proposal-permission]: **Proposal Boundary**\index{Proposal boundary!demonstration data}: The proposal boundary, defined in @sec-boundary-machine-model, separates learned proposals from the permission path that alone may admit them to the actuators (@sec-enforcement). Logging the action on both sides of it keeps permission-path interventions out of the demonstrator's labels.

A collection campaign therefore makes two decisions before it records anything: which source will choose the actions, and which of those four forms of each action the dataset will keep as its label.

## Physical Telemetry Sources and Ingestion Modalities {#sec-data-collection-sources}

A physical dataset is not found, downloaded, or passively scraped from web crawls. In disembodied AI, data pipelines scrape static text documents or curated image repositories asynchronously over HTTP, storing passive samples in cloud object stores at zero marginal physical cost. In Physical AI, every recorded transition requires moving physical mass against friction, expending electrical power, dissipating thermal energy in motor coils, and consuming mechanical fatigue life on a physical plant. The difficulty of learning from such records was visible in Dean Pomerleau's ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network) [@pomerleau1989alvinn], which attempted to learn steering policies from camera images of human driving. Because expert human drivers rarely deviated from the center of the road, the logged stream contained zero recovery trajectories from the road shoulder, causing small single-step execution errors to cascade quadratically in closed loop.

In a streaming telemetry architecture, physical data sources separate according to who chooses the action and how the control stream enters the ingestion pipeline:

1. In **kinesthetic teaching**, a colocated human demonstrator physically grasps and guides the unpowered or gravity-compensated links of the mechanism. The ingestion pipeline logs direct joint encoder displacements and passive motor back-EMF without teleoperation transport latency, but throughput is physically throttled by human muscle inertia ($1\text{--}10\text{ Hz}$) and labor cost scales strictly $1:1$ with demonstrator time. Furthermore, the demonstrator's body physically occludes camera fields of view, altering the visual distribution compared to autonomous operation.
2. In **teleoperation**, a remote operator manipulates an input device to puppet the follower robot across a network fabric.[^fn-hist-goertz-teleop] Across modern physical AI labs, four distinct teleoperation architectures dominate demonstration collection:
   - **Kinematically isomorphic leader-follower arms (e.g., bimanual ALOHA [@zhao2023learning] and GELLO [@wu2023gello]):** The operator manipulates unpowered or backdriven leader arms that duplicate the follower's link lengths and joint topologies. Joint positions stream at $50\text{ Hz}$ and copy directly to the follower without inverse kinematics (IK), eliminating mathematical singularity dead-zones. However, lack of active force reflection masks physical binding forces at the gripper.
   - **VR tracked controllers and spatial puppets (e.g., Meta Quest or HTC Vive trackers):** The operator moves 6-DoF spatial controllers in free space, streaming end-effector Cartesian poses $(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}_{\text{quat}}) \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ at $90\text{ Hz}$. A numerical IK solver converts these poses to joint targets on the follower. Optical tracking occlusion, IMU dead-reckoning drift, and IK solver singularities introduce sudden posture flips and discontinuities into the recorded control stream.
   - **Rate-controlled multi-axis space mice (e.g., 3Dconnexion):** The operator deflects an elastic 6-DoF puck to command Cartesian velocities ($\dot{\mathbf{x}} \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$). Because deflection maps to velocity rather than position, operators cannot coordinate rapid multi-joint motions and exhibit persistent step-and-wait hunting near contact surfaces.
   - **Bilateral force-reflecting master arms:** Actuated leader arms measure contact forces at the follower's wrist or load cell and actively reflect torques back into the operator's hands. While providing kinesthetic feedback, communication delay across the master-slave link risks breaking dynamic passivity, causing violent oscillatory chatter.
3. In **scripted collection**, a deterministic trajectory generator executes automated motion primitives, such as cubic splines or impedance-governed state machines. Ingestion rates are high and deterministic ($50\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$), but trajectories follow rigid, repetitive manifolds that fail to generate corrective data for off-nominal contacts, jamming when workpiece dimensions deviate by even a millimeter.
4. In **exploratory collection**, an active neural policy or reinforcement learning agent selects actions to maximize an information-theoretic objective (such as epistemic entropy or intrinsic curiosity). While data throughput matches the robot's maximum control cadence ($50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$), unbounded exploratory commands risk violent collisions, tripping safety enforcers or damaging mechanical gearboxes through repeated high-torque shock loads.
5. In **autonomous deployment logging**, production policies control the actuators during factory or warehouse operation, streaming multimodal telemetry into local circular buffers in situ. This stream provides zero-marginal-labor data at the full system execution rate ($10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ policy, $1\text{ kHz}$ joint servos), but logged states are heavily censored by runtime safety barriers and reflect only nominal operating regimes.

[^fn-hist-goertz-teleop]: **Bilateral Teleoperation Lineage**\index{Raymond Goertz!bilateral telemanipulation}: Raymond Goertz built the first bilateral master-slave telemanipulators at Argonne National Laboratory in the late 1940s and 1950s for handling radioactive materials. His linkages reflected force across a physical barrier, because operators without kinesthetic resistance jammed the remote mechanism.

### Human demonstration idiosyncrasies and mechanical artifacts {#sec-data-human-idiosyncrasies}

Teleoperation datasets do not capture pure, ideal control laws; they permanently record the physiological idiosyncrasies and biomechanical limitations of the human demonstrator:

- **Neuromuscular sub-movements and physiological tremor:** Human motor control is not a continuous, smooth spline. Neuromuscular execution operates via discrete motor unit recruitment bursts, producing intermittent corrections at $2\text{--}3\text{ Hz}$ superimposed with physiological tremor at $8\text{--}12\text{ Hz}$. When high-frequency behavioral cloning models train on raw joint velocities without low-pass filtering, the neural network learns to reproduce this neuromuscular tremor as high-frequency torque ripple, inducing rapid mechanical wear on robot gearboxes.
- **Visual latency and step-and-wait hunting:** When an operator guides a manipulator toward a contact fixture using 2D monitor displays, depth ambiguity and transport latency force the operator to adopt a *step-and-wait* control strategy: they advance the gripper a few millimeters, pause for $200\text{--}400\text{ ms}$ to visually verify contact on the video stream, and then resume motion. A policy trained on these raw pauses internalizes periodic velocity dropouts, causing the autonomous robot to stutter and freeze mid-trajectory during deployment.
- **Attentional narrowing and gaze-conditioned bias:** Human demonstrators focus visual attention narrowly on the active tool center point (TCP). Because the human's gaze does not monitor peripheral joints, elbow links often sweep close to tables or fixtures during demonstrations. A policy that imitates these demonstrations inherits elbow trajectories that flirt with the boundary of collision without possessing the demonstrator's implicit spatial awareness.

Because the source determines how the machine interacts with its physical environment, these ingestion streams occupy disjoint state-action manifolds even when executing the identical manipulation task. Consider releasing the warehouse mobile manipulator's cage-door latch. A colocated demonstrator guiding the arm feels the latch bind through direct tactile resistance and immediately modulates wrist compliance. A remote teleoperator watching compressed video streams lacks direct tactile feedback and exhibits step-and-wait hunting, pausing to visually verify strike plate contact. A scripted controller advances along a fixed geometric path at constant velocity, producing an identical, rigid contact force spike on every repetition. An exploratory policy approaches at oblique angles, binding the latch until the safety contact tripwire halts the attempt. These recorded streams are not noisy variations of a single ground-truth trajectory; they are outputs of fundamentally distinct dynamical systems characterized by divergent bandwidths, latencies, and mechanical compliance profiles, as systematized in @tbl-05-sources-taxonomy.

| Physical Data Source                     | Ingestion Bandwidth & Cadence                                                    | Contact Compliance & Force Awareness                     | Scaling Labor Economics                                     | ODD Boundary Safety Risk                                           |
|:-----------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Kinesthetic teaching**                 | Low ($1\text{--}10\text{ Hz}$, human muscle inertia)                             | High (direct physical feel of binding and compliance)    | Very high ($1:1$ dedicated human demonstrator)              | Low (demonstrator immediately feels binding forces)                |
| **Teleoperation (bilateral/isomorphic)** | Moderate ($20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$, network + human latency)                   | Moderate to high (depends on haptic force feedback)      | High ($1:1$ human operator per active cell)                 | Low to moderate (guarded by operator situational awareness)        |
| **Scripted primitives**                  | High ($50\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$, deterministic trajectory generators)           | Low (rigid trajectories unless impedance-governed)       | Low (automated once authored; engineering upfront)          | High (blind trajectory replay jams on geometric misalignments)     |
| **Exploratory policy**                   | High ($50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$, active neural exploration)                     | Variable (learned or randomized contact behaviors)       | Very low (fully autonomous hardware execution)              | Very high (unbounded exploratory actions risk destructive contact) |
| **Autonomous deployment logging**        | Full system rate ($10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ policy, $1\text{ kHz}$ joint servos) | Operational (reflects live deployed closed-loop control) | Zero marginal labor (harvested passively during production) | Guarded (governed by certified runtime safety enforcer)            |

: **Systems trade-offs across physical demonstration and telemetry sources**: Five collection sources compared across control dynamics, contact awareness, human labor economics, and physical safety risks during data capture. {#tbl-05-sources-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,20,20,20,20]"}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** The display and operator-response delay that paces a teleoperator's step-and-wait motion (@sec-data-teleop-costs) contrasts with the $1\text{ ms}$ permission tick on which each command is checked (@sec-nervous-cadences).
:::

In disembodied machine learning, empirical scaling laws correlate model performance directly with raw token count or pretraining sample volume ($N$). In cyber-physical telemetry, treating each logged control step as an independent sample is a catastrophic category error. An edge logger running at $1\text{ kHz}$ generates $3.6\times 10^6$ state-action records per hour, but adjacent records exhibit near-total temporal autocorrelation ($\rho \to 1.0$). Two kinematic records sampled one millisecond apart differ only by sub-millimeter displacements and sensor quantization noise. In statistics, the *effective sample size* (ESS) of a sequence with lag-1 autocorrelation $\rho$ scales as:
$$N_{\text{eff}} = N \frac{1 - \rho}{1 + \rho}.$$
When $\rho = 0.999$, an archive of $3.6\times 10^6$ high-frequency records carries an effective sample size of under 1,800 independent observations! Unlike text tokens in large language models, where consecutive tokens represent high-entropy semantic transitions, consecutive high-frequency robot telemetry steps contain virtually zero new information about the task manifold. Autoregressive token volume does not equal physical state-space support. Dataset coverage scales with the number of independent physical episodes, workpiece initializations, lighting conditions, and surface friction coefficients, not with the sampling clock. An archive of 500 episodes spanning diverse geometric and mechanical initial conditions provides substantially broader empirical support than 5,000,000 steps logged across repetitive passes over a single stationary fixture.

Simulation pipelines avoid the hardware wear bill and are treated in @sec-training. However, synthetic trajectories generated by rigid-body physics engines (such as MuJoCo, Isaac Sim, or Bullet) introduce severe **sim-to-real transfer artifacts**. Rigid-body simulators resolve physical contact using discrete Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) solvers or penalty-based spring-damper equations. These discrete approximations suffer from non-physical penetration of rigid geometries, instantaneous velocity jumps upon contact restitution, and simplified Coulomb friction cones that completely ignore stick-slip transitions, material viscoelasticity, and thermal friction decay. When synthetic trajectories are mixed with physical telemetry logs, every record must carry its provenance source. A neural policy trained on an undifferentiated mixture absorbs the contact-solver approximations of the physics simulator where synthetic data dominates, and absorbs motor backlash and sensor noise where physical data dominates—leaving systems engineers unable to diagnose whether an on-robot failure stems from sim-to-real transfer gaps or physical hardware degradation. A record that identifies its collection source resolves the first operational decision of a data campaign; the second decision requires specifying which form of each action signal the ingestion pipeline retains as its supervisory training target.

## Action Label Selection and Supervisory Grounding {#sec-data-action-label}

By the time the gripper contacts the strike plate on the cage-door latch, the operator's input motion has transformed into four distinct numerical signals across the system hierarchy (@fig-05-action-taps). Which signal the ingestion pipeline designates as the supervisory target determines what behavioral dynamics the neural policy internalizes. The robot splits its computational architecture across two decoupled processing domains:

- The unprivileged **Linux application processor** executes perception pipelines, handles video frame ingestion, runs teleoperation input mapping, and computes the neural policy forward pass ($\pi_\theta(o_t)$).
- On the permission side of the causal proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), a hard real-time **safety microcontroller (MCU)** executes at a deterministic $1\text{ kHz}$ cadence on bare metal, running motor field-oriented current control (FOC), joint impedance loops, and deterministic Control Barrier Functions (CBFs).[^fn-hw-encoder-capture]

[^fn-hw-encoder-capture]: **Hardware Timer Interrupt**\index{Hardware timer interrupt!DMA latching}: On real-time MCUs, encoder counts and current-shunt readings are latched by hardware timers and Direct Memory Access (DMA), which holds sampling jitter to microseconds and keeps timestamp jitter out of numerical differentiation for velocity and acceleration.

### The four-stream action tap tuple {#sec-data-four-stream-action-tap}

To capture the true causal chain of physical demonstration, an ingestion pipeline cannot log actions as single, undifferentiated vectors sampled at an arbitrary software layer. Between the moment an operator moves an input device and the moment electromagnetic torque accelerates the robot's physical links, the control signal traverses four distinct physical and algorithmic transformations. Capturing all four stages in an aligned multi-stream tuple (@fig-05-action-taps) is mandatory to prevent neural policies from conflating operator intent with actuator limitations or runtime safety interventions.

::: {#fig-05-action-taps fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Four-stream action tap tuple**: Four places a command can be logged, from raw policy intent on the application processor through to measured plant response. Which tap a dataset records decides what the model learns to imitate. Source: architectural design adapted from @zhao2023learning and @wu2023gello." fig-alt="The Four-Stream Action Tap Tuple across the Application Processor and MCU Boundary. On a heterogeneous edge architecture, data logging captures four distinct physical semantics: (1) areq (raw operator or policy intent on the Linux application processor prior to software checks), (2) acmd (kinematically retargeted setpoint), (3) aenf (safety-governed command post-CBF barrier enforcement and motor torque clamping on the MCU), and (4) ameas (measured motion derived from joint encoders over a stated response interval, with motor current logged separately). Logging only areq trains the model on commands the actuators may never have executed, while logging only ameas can misattribute mechanical compliance, link deflection, and backlash to demonstrated human skill. Source: Architectural design adapted from @zhao2023learning and @wu2023gello."}
![](images/svg/fig05_four_stream_action_taps.svg){width="100%"}
:::

As mapped across the proposal boundary in @fig-05-action-taps, logging divided between the unprivileged Linux host and the hard real-time MCU captures four distinct physical semantics:

- **Tap 1: The requested action ($a_{\text{req}}$, "Asked"):** Logged in user space on the application processor, this represents unconstrained human operator input (from a leader arm or joystick) or the raw forward-pass output from an unverified policy, tagged with its native coordinate frame and issue timestamp prior to software validation. This proposal reflects unadulterated human or policy intent, but it frequently demands infeasible joint accelerations or violates spatial bounding envelopes.
- **Tap 2: The mapped command ($a_{\text{cmd}}$, "Mapped"):** The kinematically retargeted setpoint (such as Cartesian end-effector velocities converted to joint space setpoints via inverse kinematics), incorporating coordinate frame transformations, trajectory interpolation, and workspace limits before transmission across the fieldbus.
- **Tap 3: The enforced command ($a_{\text{enf}}$, "Allowed"):** Logged on the bare-metal MCU on the permission side of the boundary, this represents the command after deterministic Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), velocity and acceleration clamps, torque saturation envelopes, and collision guards have verified or modified the proposal. This signal serves as the ground-truth supervisory label during policy training:
  $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{policy}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(o_t, a_{\text{enf}, t}) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \mathcal{D}_{\text{loss}}(\pi_\theta(o_t), a_{\text{enf}, t}) \right],$$
  guaranteeing that the model is trained exclusively on physically admissible, safety-compliant commands.
- **Tap 4: The measured response ($a_{\text{meas}}$, "Done"):** The physical plant reaction measured by optical joint encoders and motor current shunt resistors over the executed control tick, recording actual mechanical displacement and electrical effort. This measured response serves as proprioceptive state input ($o_{\text{proprio}, t+1}$) for subsequent policy steps rather than an action label.

Only this four-stream tuple, logged synchronously across the boundary between the application processor and the MCU, separates what the operator asked for from what the permission path allowed. Logging an incomplete subset creates two opposing, catastrophic distribution shifts in downstream policy learning:

- **The command-only logging trap ($a_{\text{req}}$ or $a_{\text{cmd}}$):** When a human teleoperator makes rapid, high-amplitude hand motions, the unprivileged application processor emits setpoints that exceed actuator torque-speed curves or violate safety envelopes. On the physical robot, the bare-metal microcontroller intercepts these proposals, enforcing deterministic Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and motor torque saturation limits ($a_{\text{enf}}$). The subsequent physical state $s_{t+1}$ is produced exclusively by the enforced actuation, never by the raw request. If a behavioral cloning pipeline logs only $a_{\text{req}}$ or $a_{\text{cmd}}$ as its supervisory training target, the policy is trained to emit dynamically infeasible commands that have zero causal support in the observed state transitions $(s_t, s_{t+1})$. When deployed in closed loop, this learned policy outputs aggressive commands that immediately trigger runtime safety watchdogs, trip CBF emergency braking, or overheat motor windings.
- **The response-only logging trap ($a_{\text{meas}}$):** Conversely, logging only the measured plant response records environmental resistance and transmission imperfections as if they were deliberate control targets. Consider a contact-rich manipulation task, such as seating the warehouse manipulator's gripper into a stiff cage-door latch. When the gripper contacts the strike plate, dry friction and mechanical resistance can bring joint velocities to zero ($\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\text{meas}} \approx \mathbf{0}$) while the motors deliver peak continuous holding torque. A policy trained to predict measured joint velocity ($a_{\text{meas}}$) learns that encountering contact implies commanding zero velocity—causing the robot to immediately freeze, stall, and give up forward effort the instant physical contact occurs! Furthermore, training on $a_{\text{meas}}$ bakes harmonic drive backlash, structural link deflection under heavy payloads, and external collision bounces directly into the policy weights as deliberate human demonstrations.

::: {#dfn-data-four-stream-action-tap-tuple .callout-definition title="Four-stream action tap"}

***Four-stream action tap***\index{Four-stream action tap!definition}\index{Action tap!definition} $(a_{\text{req}}, a_{\text{cmd}}, a_{\text{enf}}, a_{\text{meas}})$ is the time-synchronized multi-tier telemetry record that captures an action signal across its four causal transformation stages: unprivileged operator or policy intent ($a_{\text{req}}$), kinematically retargeted setpoint ($a_{\text{cmd}}$), safety-governed command ($a_{\text{enf}}$), and physical plant response ($a_{\text{meas}}$).

1.  **Significance**: Training imitation learning policies on raw requested actions ($a_{\text{req}}$) injects dynamically infeasible commands that trigger safety trips in deployment. Conversely, training on measured responses ($a_{\text{meas}}$) causes the model to imitate mechanical compliance, backlash, and external disturbances rather than intentional control. Logging all four streams disambiguates control intent from permission-path intervention.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike classical robot telemetry logs that capture only final motor encoder states or raw teleoperation joystick inputs, the four-stream tap preserves the exact causal filtering stages applied by intermediate software and safety hardware.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Logging streams without timestamps synchronized in hardware over the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP), written $t_{\text{PTP}}$. Even a few milliseconds of clock skew between the application processor and the MCU corrupts the temporal alignment between visual observations and corresponding torque actions.

:::

### Multi-modal time synchronization and exposure midpoint alignment {#sec-data-multimodal-time-sync}

Recording the right action tap does not settle when each recorded value was physically true. In embodied platforms, sensory modalities operate at radically disparate sampling cadences and physical propagation regimes: global-shutter cameras integrate photons over exposure windows of $10\text{--}35\text{ ms}$ at $30\text{--}60\text{ Hz}$, 6-axis force-torque sensors stream over SPI or CAN at $100\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$, optical joint encoders and field-oriented current loops execute at the MCU's deterministic $1\text{ kHz}$ tick, and neural policy models dispatch setpoints at $10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. A naive data loader that simply latches the latest available sensor sample pairs each action with a camera frame whose exposure was centered $25\text{--}40\text{ ms}$ before the frame arrived in host memory. The resulting policy learns to map historical visual states to present actions, baking artificial phase lag directly into its weights.

To quantify the physical hazard of temporal misalignment, consider the spatial tracking error $\Delta \mathbf{x}_{\text{sync}}$ injected into the dataset when an observation and an action are paired across an uncompensated phase lag $\Delta t_{\text{lag}}$:
$$\Delta \mathbf{x}_{\text{sync}}(t) = \int_{t - \Delta t_{\text{lag}}}^t \mathbf{v}(\tau)\,d\tau \approx \mathbf{v}(t) \cdot \Delta t_{\text{lag}}.$$
If a robotic manipulator moves at a nominal transit speed of $v = 0.50\text{ m/s}$, an uncorrected phase lag of $\Delta t_{\text{lag}} = 35\text{ ms}$ introduces a spatial tracking displacement of:
$$\Delta x_{\text{sync}} = 0.50\text{ m/s} \times 0.035\text{ s} = 17.5\text{ mm}.$$
In high-precision contact tasks where fixture tolerances or latch clearances are under $2\text{ mm}$, an unaligned error of $17.5\text{ mm}$ is an order of magnitude larger than the physical basin of attraction. When an imitation learning model trains on these misaligned pairs, it attempts to fit an unphysical relationship where the current action precedes the visual evidence. During closed-loop autonomous deployment, this artificial phase lag manifests as aggressive overshoot, control hunting, and severe contact chattering against rigid surfaces.

#### Hardware timestamps vs. software arrival timestamps {#sec-data-hw-vs-sw-timestamps}

The root of temporal corruption lies in conflating when an optical or electrical event occurred in physics with when the operating system kernel noticed it in software:

- **Software arrival timestamps ($t_{\text{host}}$):** In naive logging pipelines, an image frame or CAN packet is timestamped when the Linux kernel handles the device interrupt or when a user-space thread dequeues the buffer from Video4Linux2 (V4L2) or a socket. This host timestamp incorporates camera pixel readout time, USB3 or MIPI CSI-2 bus serialization, Direct Memory Access (DMA) latency, and operating system scheduling jitter:
  $$t_{\text{host}} = t_{\text{mid}} + \frac{\Delta t_{\text{exp}}}{2} + t_{\text{readout}} + t_{\text{bus}} + t_{\text{driver\_irq}} + \delta_{\text{jitter}}.$$
  Host timestamps lag physical reality by $20\text{--}45\text{ ms}$, with non-deterministic scheduling jitter ($\delta_{\text{jitter}} = \pm 5\text{--}15\text{ ms}$) driven by thread contention and CPU frequency scaling.
- **Hardware PTP timestamps ($t_{\text{PTP}}$):** Distributed robotic platforms eliminate host jitter by implementing sub-microsecond clock synchronization governed by the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP / IEEE 802.1AS). Across the real-time Ethernet fabric, a hardware Grandmaster clock exchanges timestamped sync packets with peripheral controllers. Over a two-way message transaction, the master records transmission time $t_1$ and the slave records arrival time $t_2$. The slave subsequently transmits a delay request at $t_3$, which the master receives at $t_4$. Assuming symmetric network paths, the one-way propagation delay $\tau_{\text{prop}}$ and clock offset $\theta_{\text{offset}}$ resolve as:
  $$\tau_{\text{prop}} = \frac{(t_4 - t_1) - (t_3 - t_2)}{2}, \qquad \theta_{\text{offset}} = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) - (t_4 - t_3)}{2}.$$
  Hardware timestamping at the Ethernet Physical Layer (PHY) latches packets at the physical transceiver within nanoseconds, holding clock drift between the application host, vision sensor heads, and real-time motor MCUs to under $1\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.

#### Rolling shutter skew across camera streams {#sec-data-rolling-shutter-skew}

A severe and frequently overlooked visual artifact in physical AI pipelines is **rolling shutter skew**. Low-cost consumer sensors and webcams expose pixel rows sequentially rather than instantaneously. For a sensor with $H$ vertical scanlines and line readout duration $\tau_{\text{line}}$, the exposure midpoint of row $y \in [0, H-1]$ depends linearly on its vertical coordinate:
$$t_{\text{row}}(y) = t_{\text{start}} + y \cdot \tau_{\text{line}} + \frac{\Delta t_{\text{exp}}}{2}.$$
Across a full frame, the temporal skew between the top row ($y = 0$) and bottom row ($y = H - 1$) accumulates to:
$$\Delta t_{\text{skew}} = (H - 1) \cdot \tau_{\text{line}} \approx 15\text{--}33\text{ ms}.$$
When the robot arm or camera moves at $v = 0.50\text{ m/s}$, the bottom of the manipulator in the image is captured while the physical link has displaced by up to $16.5\text{ mm}$ relative to the top of the link in the same image frame! This geometric warping (the "jello effect") deforms straight edges into curved arcs and breaks rigid-body geometry.

Crucially, in multi-camera collection rigs combining wrist-mounted and stationary third-person cameras, independent rolling shutters produce severe cross-camera asynchronous distortion. If the wrist camera scans top-to-bottom while a lateral third-person camera scans bottom-to-top, multi-view 3D vision backbones or depth triangulation pipelines receive fundamentally conflicting physical observations of the same physical instant. High-assurance physical AI collection platforms mandate **global-shutter CMOS sensors** synchronized via hardware TTL/GPIO trigger lines from the real-time MCU, ensuring that every pixel across all cameras begins and ends optical integration simultaneously at $t_{\text{mid}} = t_{\text{start}} + \Delta t_{\text{exp}} / 2$.

High-assurance data ingestion engines resolve multi-modal alignment through a three-stage real-time synchronization pipeline:

1. **Hardware-triggered optical exposure midpoint:** The real-time MCU dispatches hardware GPIO sync pulses or PTP-synchronized trigger packets to all camera global shutters simultaneously. The camera latches the trigger at $t_{\text{start}}$, and the driver calculates the true optical midpoint $t_{\text{mid}} = t_{\text{start}} + \Delta t_{\text{exp}} / 2$ in hardware PTP clock units ($t_{\text{PTP}}$), eliminating kernel driver scheduling jitter.[^fn-hw-camera-trigger]
2. **Cubic Hermite kinematic interpolation:** Because joint encoders sample at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1\text{ ms}$ period) while cameras capture at $30\text{ Hz}$ or $60\text{ Hz}$, the camera midpoint $t_{\text{mid}}$ falls between two discrete MCU telemetry ticks $t_k$ and $t_{k+1}$. An asynchronous synchronization thread interpolates joint angles $\mathbf{q}(t_{\text{mid}})$ using cubic Hermite splines across the bounding kinematic records $(t_k, \mathbf{q}_k, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_k)$ and $(t_{k+1}, \mathbf{q}_{k+1}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{k+1})$:
   $$\mathbf{q}(t_{\text{mid}}) = h_{00}(u) \mathbf{q}_k + h_{10}(u) \Delta t_s \dot{\mathbf{q}}_k + h_{01}(u) \mathbf{q}_{k+1} + h_{11}(u) \Delta t_s \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{k+1},$$
   where $\Delta t_s = t_{k+1} - t_k = 1\text{ ms}$, $u = (t_{\text{mid}} - t_k)/\Delta t_s \in [0, 1]$, and $h_{ij}(u)$ are the cubic Hermite basis functions (@sec-appendix-control-splines). This ensures $C^1$ continuity and eliminates the artificial high-frequency velocity jumps produced by nearest-neighbor zero-order hold latching.
3. **Pre-serialization alignment:** Container formats store multi-rate topics with the timestamps provided by the logger. Temporal alignment must occur in volatile shared memory buffers before records are serialized to disk, guaranteeing that every image frame is bound to the exact kinematic state that existed when the photons hit the silicon sensor.

[^fn-hw-camera-trigger]: **Hardware optical exposure triggering**: Software USB triggers (such as V4L2 ioctl calls) introduce variable kernel scheduling jitter of $\pm 5\,\text{ms}$. To eliminate temporal uncertainty, high-assurance collection rigs utilize dedicated hardware GPIO or TTL sync pulses generated by the real-time microcontroller. This aligns global shutters across multi-camera rigs to within microseconds.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Sub-microsecond PTP clock synchronization across distributed bus controllers is established in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses.
:::

### Standardized demonstration storage containers and serialization formats {#sec-data-storage-containers}

Aligning multi-rate telemetry settles timing, but storing it for high-throughput training introduces contrasting I/O requirements across four primary physical AI container architectures:

- **MCAP (Foxglove):** A modular, append-only binary container format engineered specifically for robotics pub/sub logging. MCAP supports zero-copy streaming of heterogeneous, multi-rate topics (such as 30 Hz RGB-D frames, 100 Hz IMU packets, and 1 kHz actuator states). Because its index is appended sequentially to the end of the file, MCAP is completely crash-resilient: if a robot suffers abrupt power loss or an operating system kernel panic during data collection, the recorded stream remains intact up to the final byte without corrupting container headers.
- **Zarr / HDF5:** Chunked, N-dimensional compressed array formats optimized for dense numeric tensors. While HDF5 is widely used in scientific computing, ungraceful power loss corrupts its root metadata tree, and internal file locking limits multi-threaded concurrent writers. Zarr replaces monolithic files with directory hierarchies of sharded chunks, making it robust for cloud object storage and high-throughput random-access slicing during policy training, but requiring pre-synchronized, fixed-rate tabular inputs.
- **LeRobot (Hugging Face / Parquet + Video):** An embodied AI storage format that decouples tabular kinematic data from high-bandwidth visual streams [@cadene2024lerobot]. Kinematic states and action taps are serialized into Apache Parquet columnar files, while video streams are compressed into MP4/AV1 containers. This hybrid layout maintains small file sizes and allows PyTorch DataLoaders to ingest lightweight kinematics instantly while delegating video decompression to dedicated hardware decoders. Crucially, inter-frame codecs (such as H.264, H.265, and AV1) use Group-of-Pictures (GOP) temporal compression. While this achieves 20- to 50-fold file size reduction, randomly shuffling demonstration episodes during PyTorch DataLoader training causes severe CPU/GPU pipeline stalls: decoding a single random step requires seeking to the preceding I-frame and decompressing the entire GOP sequence, starving training throughput. High-throughput training pipelines therefore often favor intra-frame codecs (such as ProRes or intra-only MJPEG), which decode every frame independently in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time at the expense of higher disk storage.
- **RLDS / TFRecord (Open X-Embodiment):** A protocol-buffer-based episode format structuring trajectories into nested step dictionaries (`is_first`, `is_last`, `observation`, `action`, `discount`) [@open_x_embodiment_collaboration2024open]. RLDS is engineered for distributed Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) and multi-node GPU clusters, enabling petabyte-scale streaming across massive heterogeneous multi-embodiment corpora.

A tap and a timestamp are only as good as the loop that produced them. In teleoperation, still the standard way to gather high-quality physical trajectories, that loop runs through a human, and the interface between human and machine shapes the recorded dynamics long before the data reaches a model.

## Teleoperation Demonstration Costs {#sec-data-teleop-costs}

In physical data engineering, teleoperation is not merely a manual control mechanism—it is an end-to-end, asynchronous cyber-physical data generation pipeline with a human in the loop (@fig-05-teleop-rig). A workspace camera captures the physical scene and streams encoded frames across a network fabric to an operator console; the human operator perceives the visual display, cognitively decides on a trajectory correction, and displaces an input device; the host workstation maps that motion into a kinematically retargeted setpoint and transmits it across a fieldbus to the motor drives; the actuators accelerate the robot's physical links against inertia, friction, and environmental contact; and the updated scene arrives at the camera sensor on the subsequent cycle.

::: {#fig-05-teleop-rig fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation rigs**: Demonstration capture on three leader-follower rigs whose leader devices mirror follower kinematics [@wu2023gello]. Because the leader shares the follower's joint structure, the interface needs no inverse kinematics and inherits none of its singularities (mathematical dead-zones where joints align and lose mobility), preserving the operator's direct joint-level coordination. The operator's continuous-correction latency still enters the recording as phase lag, so the demonstration carries the operator's delay as if it were policy." fig-alt="Kinematically Isomorphic Leader-Follower Teleoperation Architecture across Heterogeneous Manipulators. Demonstration acquisition on physical robot platforms using low-cost, kinematically isomorphic leader controllers (canonical architecture [@wu2023gello]). (A) Bimanual teleoperation setup with twin 6-DoF leader arms mapped directly to dual heavy-payload follower manipulators during a compliant liquid-pouring task. (B) Single-arm leader-follower configuration controlling a torque-controlled manipulator with an overhead task camera. (C) Precision pick-and-place manipulation with passive gravity compensation and joint-angle direct drive. Because the leader device mirrors follower kinematics without requiring numerical inverse kinematics (IK), the interface eliminates IK singularities while preserving the operator's direct joint-level coordination. However, the operator's continuous-correction latency and communication delays still introduce phase lag into the recorded (st, at) demonstration tuples. Source: Adapted from Wu et al. [@wu2023gello], CC BY 4.0."}
![](images/png/fig05_real_gello_teleop.png){width="95%"}
:::

As shown across the three physical systems in @fig-05-teleop-rig, kinematically isomorphic leader rigs (such as GELLO [@wu2023gello]) duplicate the joint layout of the follower robot on the operator's desk:

- In **Panel (a)**, a bimanual setup maps twin 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) 3D-printed leader arms directly to dual industrial manipulators during a compliant liquid-pouring task.
- In **Panel (b)**, a single-arm setup guides a compliant torque-controlled arm using an overhead camera for visual alignment.
- In **Panel (c)**, a precision pick-and-place station uses passive joint counterbalancing to eliminate operator muscle fatigue without adding active motors.

Because each leader joint angle maps directly to the corresponding follower joint angle ($\mathbf{q}_{\text{leader}} \equiv \mathbf{q}_{\text{follower}}$), the interface avoids numerical inverse kinematics (IK) entirely, bypassing kinematic singularities where joints align and lose degrees of freedom. However, the operator's visual-neuromuscular reaction latency ($t_{\text{hum}} \approx 200\,\text{ms}$) and transport delay still enter the recording as phase lag.

### Human-in-the-loop latency and bilateral passivity breakdown {#sec-data-bilateral-passivity}

Each stage in this distributed loop introduces latency that affects the timing of the correction. In a reference setup with a high-speed camera and a wired local network (illustrative; see the Reader Guide), display processing requires $t_{\text{disp}} = 50\text{ ms}$ across exposure integration, H.264 decoding, and monitor raster refresh. Human visual perception, cognitive motor planning, and neuromuscular transmission introduce an operator response latency of $t_{\text{hum}} = 200\text{ ms}$ for continuous path corrections. Command quantization, packetization, and bus transport to the robot controller add $t_{\text{cmd}} = 10\text{ ms}$. Actuator torque ramp-up and structural inertia impose a mechanical response latency of $t_{\text{mech}} = 80\text{ ms}$ before the robot achieves the commanded acceleration. The **teleoperation round-trip latency** $t_{\text{loop}}$, the time from a contact event to the corrective actuator response, is their sum:
$$t_{\text{loop}} = t_{\text{disp}} + t_{\text{hum}} + t_{\text{cmd}} + t_{\text{mech}} = 50\text{ ms} + 200\text{ ms} + 10\text{ ms} + 80\text{ ms} = 340\text{ ms}.$$

When a contact misalignment occurs at time $t$, the operator sees it on the display at $t + 50\text{ ms}$, commands a physical correction at $t + 250\text{ ms}$, and the arm pushes back at $t + 340\text{ ms}$, while the arm keeps moving under momentum and contact forces. A logger that naively pairs the observation $s_t$ with the command issued at the same instant pairs a state with an action chosen for a state $250\text{ ms}$ older. The policy learns that delay as deliberate behavior and over-corrects or oscillates when it runs autonomously at the control rate. The round-trip latency is therefore a property of the dataset, not only of the rig, because it enters every demonstration as phase lag dominated by the operator's own reaction time.

When contact force is reflected back to the operator's hand in **bilateral teleoperation**, transmission delay becomes a dynamic stability hazard. In an ideal passive physical system, energy cannot be generated out of thin air: the mechanical work performed by the slave robot on the environment must be bounded by the work delivered by the human operator. In bilateral teleoperation across a delayed link, however, the operator commands velocity $v(t)$ at the master handle while the remote environment reflects delayed contact force $F_{\text{contact}}(t - \tau)$ back to the master motors. Over a periodic oscillatory cycle of period $T_{\text{cycle}}$, the net mechanical energy $\Delta E$ injected by the delayed communication link into the master-slave coupling is governed by the work-energy integral:
$$\Delta E = \int_0^{T_{\text{cycle}}} F_{\text{contact}}(t - \tau) v(t)\,dt.$$
As Anderson and Spong demonstrated [@anderson1989bilateral], when transmission delay $\tau > 0$ introduces a phase shift between reflected force and operator velocity, the force vector aligns with velocity ($F(t-\tau) \cdot v(t) > 0$), resulting in net positive energy generation ($\Delta E > 0$). The delayed communication channel ceases to act as an inert transmission line; it acts as an active physical energy source! This injected energy drives the coupled leader-follower mechanism into self-excited, unstable limit-cycle oscillations against rigid contact surfaces—manifesting as violent haptic chatter that can shatter gearboxes or injure operators (@sec-appendix-control-passivity).

To restore passivity, classical architectures deploy wave-variable transformations or time-domain passivity observers (TDPC) that monitor energy flow and inject virtual damping $\Delta B$ whenever $\Delta E > 0$. However, this virtual damping acts as a heavy low-pass filter on the reflected force, attenuating high-frequency tactile transients and masking the crisp contact cues required for precision assembly demonstrations. For an ML systems data pipeline, this exposes an irreconcilable trade-off: unfiltered force reflection risks physical instability and operator injury during demonstration collection, whereas passivity-enforcing damping strips the recorded tactile telemetry of the sharp contact gradients required to train high-precision insertion and assembly policies.

The interface thus filters what a demonstration can express. A force-reflecting leader lets the operator feel binding; a visual-only rate controller encourages short moves and pauses while the operator checks the video. A backdriven joint-space leader such as ALOHA, recorded at $50\text{ Hz}$ [@zhao2023learning], sits between them, conveying the leader's mechanical feel without follower force. With any of these interfaces, operators slow down near contact, because a high-gain loop closed around $t_{\text{loop}}$ would lose its phase margin. @Tbl-05-teleop-taxonomy lists these behaviors as artifacts to check on a given rig rather than as universal ranges.

| Interface and feedback                                        | Command mapping                                                                      | Contact information available to operator                                  | Possible collection artifact to check                                             |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Force-reflecting bilateral leader**                         | Leader motion mapped to follower joints; measured follower force reflected to leader | Vision and physical contact force, subject to link delay and fidelity      | Contact corrections and oscillation when delayed force reflection loses passivity |
| **Backdriven joint-space leader (ALOHA)** [@zhao2023learning] | Leader joint positions copied to follower; demonstration recorded at $50\text{ Hz}$  | Vision and leader mechanism feel, without active follower force reflection | Joint-space posture preferences and unobserved follower contact forces            |
| **Rate-controlled 3D mouse**                                  | Device deflection mapped to Cartesian velocity, then inverse kinematics              | Primarily visual feedback unless a separate haptic channel exists          | Step-and-wait motion and zero-velocity pauses under delayed feedback              |
| **Tracked spatial controller**                                | Tracked hand pose mapped to tool pose with clutching and scale                       | Visual feedback; optional vibration is not directional force reflection    | Clutch discontinuities and pose-tracking gaps                                     |
| **Instrumented exoskeleton**                                  | Wearable joint motion retargeted to robot joints                                     | Depends on whether active force feedback is fitted                         | Biomechanical calibration and retargeting bias                                    |

: **Teleoperation interface mechanisms for physical demonstration collection**: Mapping and feedback determine what the operator can demonstrate, and the last column names the artifact to check on a given rig, task, and operator. {#tbl-05-teleop-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[22,28,24,26]"}

### High-throughput telemetry ingestion and storage hierarchy {#sec-data-telemetry-ingestion-storage}

Whatever interface the operator holds, the collection rig must record every stream the session produces, including all four action taps of \ref{dfn-data-four-stream-action-tap-tuple}, high-rate joint torques, and multi-view video. Ingesting this firehose exposes a fundamental systems trade-off between edge write bandwidth during data capture and random-access decode latency during policy training:

- **Intra-frame codecs (MJPEG, Apple ProRes):** Compress each frame independently. While this yields moderate compression ratios ($\sim 8\times$, sustaining $\sim 390\,\text{MB/s}$ on a multi-camera rig), it provides $\mathcal{O}(1)$ random seek times with negligible CPU overhead during PyTorch DataLoader batch generation.
- **Inter-frame codecs (H.264, H.265 / HEVC):** Achieve high compression ratios ($\sim 20\text{--}50\times$) by exploiting temporal redundancy across Groups of Pictures (GOPs). However, extracting an arbitrary historical frame $s_t$ during random episode shuffling forces the host CPU or GPU hardware decoder to decompress the entire preceding GOP (typically 15 to 60 frames), causing severe DataLoader worker stalls and starving the training accelerator.

Sizing the raw ingestion pipeline against physical NVMe and SATA storage bandwidth determines whether the collection computer can stream multi-modal telemetry without dropping frames.

```{python}
#| label: calc-data-multi-camera-ingestion
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MULTI-CAMERA TELEOPERATION INGESTION BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-data-ingestion-bandwidth-storage-budgets-multi-camera
# │ Goal:    Size the raw ingestion rate and storage of one teleoperated
# │          door-opening session on the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show:    Per-camera raw rates, the 9-axis kinematic stream, the total, the
# │          hourly and per-shift storage, and the 8x-compressed rate against
# │          SATA and Gen4 NVMe write bandwidth.
# │ How:     Camera geometry and frame rates from the registry (navigation
# │          IMX477, wrist IMX296, two external RealSense D435i); axis count and
# │          logging rate from RM; calc_teleop_ingestion_budget per camera group.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory, fmt_frequency, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class MultiCameraIngestionBudget:
    """Raw telemetry bandwidth and storage for the machine's teleoperation sessions."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    cam_nav = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet
    cam_wrist = RM.wrist_camera  # category: datasheet
    cam_ext = Sensors.Camera.Intel_RealSense_D435i  # category: datasheet
    n_ext = 2  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    bytes_per_px_rgb = 3  # 24-bit RGB after debayering; category: chosen
    bytes_per_px_depth = 2  # uint16 depth aligned to the color frame; category: chosen

    n_axes = RM.servo_axes  # 2 base + 7 arm; category: datasheet
    f_log = RM.permission_rate  # kinematics logged every permission tick; category: chosen
    values_per_axis = 6  # position, velocity (a_meas), torque, a_req, a_cmd, a_enf; category: chosen
    bytes_per_value = 4  # float32; category: chosen
    bytes_timestamp = 8  # one 64-bit timestamp per step; category: chosen

    shift_hours = 8.0  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    compression_ratio = 8.0  # intra-frame video codec; category: illustrative
    bw_sata = Systems.Storage.SataSsd.bandwidth  # category: datasheet
    bw_nvme = Hardware.Tech.Storage.NvmeGen4.bandwidth  # category: datasheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_step = n_axes * values_per_axis * bytes_per_value + bytes_timestamp
    bw_kin = (bytes_per_step * byte * f_log).to(MB / second)

    res_nav = calc_teleop_ingestion_budget(
        num_cameras=1,
        rgb_width=cam_nav.resolution_width,
        rgb_height=cam_nav.resolution_height,
        rgb_fps=cam_nav.frame_rate.to(hertz).magnitude,
        rgb_bytes_per_pixel=bytes_per_px_rgb,
        kinematics_bytes_per_sec=bw_kin,
    )
    res_wrist = calc_teleop_ingestion_budget(
        num_cameras=1,
        rgb_width=cam_wrist.resolution_width,
        rgb_height=cam_wrist.resolution_height,
        rgb_fps=cam_wrist.frame_rate.to(hertz).magnitude,
        rgb_bytes_per_pixel=bytes_per_px_rgb,
    )
    res_ext = calc_teleop_ingestion_budget(
        num_cameras=n_ext,
        rgb_width=cam_ext.resolution_width,
        rgb_height=cam_ext.resolution_height,
        rgb_fps=cam_ext.frame_rate.to(hertz).magnitude,
        rgb_bytes_per_pixel=bytes_per_px_rgb,
        depth_width=cam_ext.resolution_width,
        depth_height=cam_ext.resolution_height,
        depth_fps=cam_ext.frame_rate.to(hertz).magnitude,
        depth_bytes_per_pixel=bytes_per_px_depth,
    )

    bw_nav = res_nav["bw_rgb"]
    bw_wrist = res_wrist["bw_rgb"]
    bw_ext_rgb = res_ext["bw_rgb"]
    bw_ext_depth = res_ext["bw_depth"]
    bw_ext = res_ext["bw_vision"]
    bw_total = (res_nav["bw_total"] + res_wrist["bw_total"] + res_ext["bw_total"]).to(MB / second)
    storage_hour = (res_nav["storage_per_hour"] + res_wrist["storage_per_hour"] + res_ext["storage_per_hour"]).to(TB)
    storage_shift = (storage_hour * shift_hours).to(TB)

    nav_over_sata = (bw_nav / bw_sata).to("").magnitude
    kin_share = (bw_kin / bw_total).to("").magnitude
    bw_compressed = (bw_total / compression_ratio).to(MB / second)
    storage_hour_compressed = (storage_hour / compression_ratio).to(TB)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_axes == 9, "The machine logs 9 axes (2 base, 7 arm)")
    check(bytes_per_step == 224, "Unexpected kinematic record size")
    check(abs(bw_kin.to(MB / second).magnitude - 0.224) < 1e-9, "Unexpected kinematic rate")
    check(abs(bw_nav.to(MB / second).magnitude - 2219.44) < 0.01, "Unexpected navigation-camera rate")
    check(abs(bw_wrist.to(MB / second).magnitude - 279.94) < 0.01, "Unexpected wrist-camera rate")
    check(abs(bw_ext.to(MB / second).magnitude - 622.08) < 0.01, "Unexpected external-camera rate")
    check(abs(bw_total.to(MB / second).magnitude - 3121.68) < 0.01, "Unexpected total ingestion rate")
    check(abs(storage_hour.to(TB).magnitude - 11.24) < 0.005, "Unexpected hourly storage")
    check(abs(storage_shift.to(TB).magnitude - 89.91) < 0.01, "Unexpected shift storage")
    check(bw_total < bw_nvme, "Raw ingestion must fit Gen4 NVMe write bandwidth")
    check(3.9 < nav_over_sata < 4.1, "Navigation camera alone should be about four times SATA")
    check(kin_share < 1e-4, "Kinematic stream should be under 0.01 percent of the bytes")
    check(abs(bw_compressed.to(MB / second).magnitude - 390.2) < 0.1, "Unexpected compressed rate")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    nav_w_str = fmt_int(cam_nav.resolution_width, commas=False)
    nav_h_str = fmt_int(cam_nav.resolution_height, commas=False)
    nav_fps_str = fmt_frequency(cam_nav.frame_rate, precision=0)
    wrist_w_str = fmt_int(cam_wrist.resolution_width, commas=False)
    wrist_h_str = fmt_int(cam_wrist.resolution_height, commas=False)
    wrist_fps_str = fmt_frequency(cam_wrist.frame_rate, precision=0)
    ext_w_str = fmt_int(cam_ext.resolution_width, commas=False)
    ext_h_str = fmt_int(cam_ext.resolution_height, commas=False)
    ext_fps_str = fmt_frequency(cam_ext.frame_rate, precision=0)
    n_ext_str = fmt_int(n_ext)
    n_axes_str = fmt_int(n_axes)
    f_log_str = fmt_frequency(f_log, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
    bytes_per_step_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_step)

    bw_nav_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_nav, unit=MB / second, precision=2)
    bw_wrist_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_wrist, unit=MB / second, precision=2)
    bw_ext_rgb_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_ext_rgb, unit=MB / second, precision=2)
    bw_ext_depth_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_ext_depth, unit=MB / second, precision=2)
    bw_ext_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_ext, unit=MB / second, precision=2)
    bw_kin_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_kin, unit=MB / second, precision=2)
    bw_total_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_total, unit=MB / second, precision=2)
    bw_total_gb_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_total, unit=GB / second, precision=2)
    storage_hour_str = fmt_memory(storage_hour, unit=TB, precision=2)
    storage_shift_str = fmt_memory(storage_shift, unit=TB, precision=1)
    shift_hours_str = fmt_int(int(shift_hours))

    bw_sata_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_sata, unit=MB / second, precision=0)
    bw_nvme_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_nvme, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    nav_over_sata_mult_str = fmt_multiple(nav_over_sata, precision=1)
    kin_share_str = fmt_percent(kin_share, precision=3)
    compression_mult_str = fmt_multiple(compression_ratio, precision=0)
    bw_compressed_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw_compressed, unit=MB / second, precision=1)
    storage_hour_compressed_str = fmt_memory(storage_hour_compressed, unit=TB, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-data-ingestion-bandwidth-storage-budgets-multi-camera .callout-notebook title="Multi-camera ingestion and storage budgets"}
**Question**: What sustained ingestion rate and storage does one teleoperated door-opening session on the warehouse mobile manipulator generate when every camera and every axis is logged raw?

**Parameters** (camera geometry is datasheet; logging formats are chosen):

- **Navigation camera:** `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.nav_w_str` by `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.nav_h_str` px at `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.nav_fps_str`, logged as 24-bit RGB ($3\text{ bytes/px}$).
- **Wrist camera:** `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.wrist_w_str` by `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.wrist_h_str` px at `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.wrist_fps_str`, logged the same way.
- **External cameras:** `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.n_ext_str` RGB-D cameras viewing the door, color at `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.ext_w_str` by `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.ext_h_str` px and `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.ext_fps_str`, with depth aligned to the color frame as raw `uint16` millimeters ($2\text{ bytes/px}$).
- **Kinematics:** `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.n_axes_str` axes (two base wheels, seven arm joints) logged at `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.f_log_str`. Each step stores, for every axis, position and velocity (the measured response $a_{\text{meas}}$), measured torque, and the requested, mapped, and enforced commands as 32-bit values, plus one 64-bit timestamp, for `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bytes_per_step_str` bytes per step.

**Calculation**:

1. **Raw video bandwidth:** the navigation camera streams `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_nav_str` and the wrist camera `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_wrist_str`. The external pair adds `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_ext_rgb_str` of color and `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_ext_depth_str` of depth, `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_ext_str` in all.
2. **Kinematic bandwidth:** `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bytes_per_step_str` bytes per step at `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.f_log_str` is `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_kin_str`.
3. **Total sustained ingestion rate:** the streams sum to `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_total_str`, about `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_total_gb_str`.
4. **Hourly and shift storage consumption:** uncompressed telemetry accumulates at `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.storage_hour_str` per hour, or `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.storage_shift_str` across a `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.shift_hours_str`-hour collection shift on one machine.

**Systems insight**:
The navigation camera alone writes `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.nav_over_sata_mult_str` what a SATA SSD sustains (`{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_sata_str`). The full session fits within a Gen4 NVMe drive's `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_nvme_str`, but only by consuming storage at `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.storage_hour_str` per hour. Intra-frame video compression at an illustrative `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.compression_mult_str` brings the rate to about `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.bw_compressed_str` (`{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.storage_hour_compressed_str` per hour) at the cost of encoder latency and artifacts in the frames the policy will train on. The kinematic stream, which carries all four action taps, is `{python} MultiCameraIngestionBudget.kin_share_str` percent of the bytes. The record that preserves the causal chain is the cheapest stream to log, so a logger that drops data under buffer pressure must never drop it first.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_sensory_ingestion_bandwidth_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder comparing camera raw bandwidth against USB, SATA, and NVMe bus ceilings."}

*Multi-camera raw telemetry overwhelms legacy storage interfaces, requiring direct PCIe NVMe logging.*
:::

### Operational yield and mechanical fatigue budgeting {#sec-data-yield-fatigue-budgeting}

Raw storage bandwidth bounds how much telemetry an edge rig can physically capture; operational yield and hardware durability bound how much validated data a campaign can produce.
